supporting_cards.title: Position a local business against the giant's size weakness, then make operations match the promise
supporting_cards.summary: United Jersey became the 'fast-moving bank' by exploiting big New York banks' slow service and backing the ad promise with seven concrete operational commitments.
supporting_cards.use_when: Positioning a smaller store or local brand against a large national competitor whose weakness is slowness or bureaucracy.
steps: Study the competition, not yourself, to find the position, as Tylenol did by studying aspirin's problems rather than its own product.

Target the competitors who actually occupy the prospect's mind, not smaller rivals nobody thinks about — the source chose the big New York banks because 'positioning is always a question of dealing with what's in the mind.'
Name the leader's real weakness: large size means slow reaction time, similar to the Avis 'shorter line' claim.

Before advertising the promise, change operations to deliver it. United Jersey made seven commitments: decentralized decisions (a lending team can approve a $10 million loan, meeting daily), cross-training staff so questions aren't referred elsewhere, statewide ATM commitment, six-times-daily lock box pickups, FACT terminals for fast merchant approvals, responsiveness on rates and products, and a Princeton headquarters central to all customers.

Only then run the promise-based advertising. TV spots contrasted United Jersey bankers with the fictional 'Lethargic National Bank,' and print used headlines like 'Haste makes money' and 'Banks shouldn't hold up people.'
Reinforce internally with 'Time Is Money' desk signs for officers.

Track awareness and attitude, not just sales. The source reports unaided awareness nearly tripled in just over a year and one officer noted line officers were visibly striving to live up to the promise.
caveats: The reported earnings increase of $30 million (26%) is a specific case result, not a general expectation.
The source's essence criterion is that a good position transcends every aspect of the company — if operations can't match the ad, the strategy fails.
supporting_cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

supporting_cards.title: Decide whether a tagline earns a place in the store's messaging
supporting_cards.summary: Taglines are shorthand for the brand promise; keep one only if it is short, differentiated, memorable and consistent with actual delivery.
supporting_cards.use_when: When writing or reviewing a store's tagline, homepage hero line, packaging promise or recurring campaign line.
steps: Check the essentials: short, differentiated from competitors, unique, captures brand essence and positioning, easy to say and remember, no negative connotations, displayed in a small font, protectable and trademarkable, and evokes an emotional response.

Classify the tagline type to ensure fit: imperative (commands action, usually starts with a verb — Nike 'Just do it', TOMS 'One for One'); descriptive (states the service, product or promise — BMW 'The ultimate driving machine'); superlative (positions as best in class, e.g. Budweiser 'King of beers'); provocative (thought-provoking, often a question — eBay 'Where else?'); or specific (reveals the business category).
Confirm the tagline is a brand promise you can actually deliver — the source cites Target's 'Expect More, Pay Less' as a promise to consumers.
Plan for long use and frequent, consistent repetition; the source says the best taglines have a long life and transcend changes in the marketplace and lifestyle.
Expect taglines to have shorter life spans than logos historically, but do not use that as license to change them casually — repetition is what builds meaning.
caveats: Tagline examples are illustrative, not evidence that a similar line will lift sales.
Protectability matters; verify trademark status if the line is central to your packaging or campaigns.

supporting_cards.title: Map positioning on an extreme emotional XY grid
supporting_cards.summary: Use unconventional emotional axes (not price vs features) to find a defensible positioning space.
supporting_cards.use_when: Choosing how to differentiate your store or product line in a crowded category.
steps: Pick two extreme emotional attributes your category actually competes on — for example speed vs security, or status vs convenience.
Plot competitors on the two axes to see where the crowded middle sits; the middle is usually where undifferentiated brands die.
Choose a corner position that is extreme on at least one axis rather than a balanced compromise.
Define the brand promise so it clearly attracts the customers who want that extreme and repels the ones who don't.
Use the chosen position to guide merchandising, PDP messaging, and which product attributes you lead with — not just ads.
Revisit the grid when you add categories; an extreme position can carry across lines or may need its own grid.
caveats: Source uses these as strategic frames, not quantified scores; the axes are chosen judgment calls, not measured data.
An extreme position intentionally repels some buyers; that exclusion is the point, not a flaw.

supporting_cards.title: Keep the brand speaking with one voice across channels
supporting_cards.summary: 'Stay on message' means the same distinctive voice and unified message across web, social, sales conversation and leadership communication, centered on the customer.
supporting_cards.use_when: When assigning copy across store pages, emails, packaging inserts and social posts, or fixing inconsistency after multiple teams and freelancers have written content.
steps: Inventory the language assets the source lists, so nothing is left to improvisation: nomenclature (formal and informal company name, taglines, descriptors, product/process/service/division names), brand essence, mission and vision statements, value propositions, key messages, guiding principles, customer pledges, vocabulary, history, boilerplate and elevator speech.
Standardize voice and tone rules: headline style, punctuation, capitalization, emphasis, and the standard for accuracy, clarity and consistency.
Cover information mechanics too: calls to action, phone numbers, URLs, email signatures, voicemail, abbreviations, titles, addresses and directions.

Apply the same discipline across touchpoints the source enumerates: websites and blogs, news releases, FAQs, press kits, brochures, shareholder communications, call-center and sales scripts, presentations, announcements, blast emails, ad campaigns, direct mail, product directions, signage and apps.
Write so the message is vital, straightforward, eloquent and substantive, and accessible to all customers; cut through hype and clutter.
Accept that unified messaging requires buy-in at all levels and long-term commitment — repetition is what makes a message memorable.
caveats: Consistency requires ongoing governance; one style guide alone does not enforce it.
The source notes a busy reader may spend only minutes, so prioritize clarity and brevity over completeness in any single message.

supporting_cards.title: Strip Technical Jargon from Product and Marketing Copy
supporting_cards.summary: Write a brand voice that is human, confident and clear even in a technical product category
supporting_cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, specs pages, emails or ads for a technically complex product where copy has drifted into insider language
steps: Set the target balance explicitly. The source's stated goal was professional but not corporate, friendly but not fake, and it describes this as a difficult balance to strike — write the two poles down as a copy review test.

Assume your buyer is not a specialist. Even though the keyboard world is full of technical jargon, the source makes a conscious effort to use clear, simple language anyone can understand, on the reasoning that newcomers and enthusiasts both need to buy.

Draft core messages collaboratively in a shared document and refine them over multiple passes. Mode used a Notion document to write and refine core messages so word choices felt authentic rather than imposed.

Ban marketing buzzwords and favor honest, straightforward communication. Keep the emotional promise concrete — the source's themes were 'making technology feel more human and inviting' and 'creating joy in everyday experiences', expressed plainly rather than as abstract brandspeak.

Produce messaging samples attached to specific placements (website, marketing) rather than a general tone document, and keep a separate set of thought-starter 'brand expressions' showing the voice applied across physical and digital surfaces for future launches and events.
caveats: Voice work was done by an internal team with an outside facilitator; a solo operator should expect more drafting rounds to reach the same clarity.
Simplifying does not mean removing necessary specs — the source keeps deep technical information available for research-heavy buyers and reserves simple language for messaging.
supporting_cards.source_name: Building a Brand – Redesigning a Business Start to Finish.docx

supporting_cards.title: Use semiotics and vernacular to signal tribe belonging
supporting_cards.summary: Deliberate symbols, category vernacular, and visual cues attract the right tribe and filter out the wrong people.
supporting_cards.use_when: Designing PDP imagery, packaging, tone of voice, or ad creative that should signal who the product is for.
steps: Identify the trusted visual and verbal patterns your target tribe already recognizes in the category (source example draws on cues like driving gloves with holes or car wheel flares).
Embed those recognizable signifiers in your product photography, copy, and design rather than inventing unfamiliar signals.
Use intentional signals to attract insiders and repel outsiders — the source cites spam with deliberate bad grammar as a filter that selects only the gullible.
Match tone and vernacular to the tribe's own language so the store feels like 'people like us' rather than an outsider.
Audit existing assets for signals that attract the wrong audience or dilute the tribe signal.
Keep symbols coherent across PDP, email, packaging, and ads so the signal compounds.
caveats: Semiotic choices are interpretive and category-specific; what signals insider status in one tribe reads as noise or offense in another.
Over-filtering can shrink your addressable audience — the source treats this as a feature, but confirm demand exists.

supporting_cards.title: Consistency is a brand promise; authenticity is for amateurs
supporting_cards.summary: Deliver the promised version of your brand on every touchpoint regardless of how you feel, because customers bought the promise, not your mood.
supporting_cards.use_when: Customer service standards, shipping and fulfillment consistency, and repeat-touchpoint design such as subscriptions, email and support responses.
steps: Adopt the source's rule: 'authenticity is for amateurs, consistency is for professionals' — customers don't want your authentic bad day, they want the version of you that you promised them.
Apply the hotel illustration: a doorman having an authentically bad day is not what a guest wants; a messy room because the housekeeper was authentic is not an acceptable service outcome.

For subscriptions and replenishment: the performer's example is that if you're sick of playing your hit, don't tour — or if you tour, you give the audience what they signed up for instead of switching to classical music unannounced.
Set explicit brand promises (delivery time, packaging, response time, product quality) and hold them even when it's inconvenient, because that is what a brand is.
Keep the source's boundary: don't do work you're not proud of or work that burns you out — consistency is not the same as enduring a bad business.
caveats: The source addresses pushback directly: we have been non-authentic since age two (driving 20mph with cars ahead), so this is not a demand to fake your whole identity — it is a service standard.
This is a strong norm stated by the source; there are legitimate brand positions built on raw authenticity, and the choice is situational.
supporting_cards.source_name: Marketing Godfather_ How To Build An Audience That Buys (Best Hour You’ll Spend Today!) _ Seth Godin.docx

supporting_cards.title: Apply the cigarette fMRI finding to replenishment and cue design
supporting_cards.summary: Logo-free brand-associated imagery triggered more craving activity than explicit product or logo imagery among smokers.
supporting_cards.use_when: Replenishment triggers, retention email design, or subscription reactivation campaigns for habitual or consumable products.
steps: The study showed that logo-free cues associated with a cigarette brand — a red Ferrari, cowboys, a sunset — produced more activity in reward/craving regions than logos or pack images did. Lindstrom reports the effect was consistent for both Marlboro and Camel smokers and lasted under five seconds of exposure.
Translate to your category: identify sensory or visual cues your regular buyers already associate with using your product (the mug, the scent, the setting, the routine).
Use those cue-only assets in replenishment emails and push notifications ('time to restock', 'your morning') rather than pasting a product logo or price banner on every message.

Keep cues consistent over time so they accumulate association — the source describes years of tobacco marketing building the link between race imagery and the cigarette brands before the association took hold.
For repeated-purchase conversion, test cue-only creative against logo-plus-product creative on reorder rate, not on initial open rate.
caveats: The craving-region fMRI findings are specific to nicotine-dependent smokers viewing tobacco cues; craving is not the same mechanism as ordinary purchase intent.
Cross-category association building takes years of consistent spend; a single campaign will not produce the same effect.
Lindstrom's finding is presented as a research result within his own lab, not an industry benchmark.

foundation_candidates.title: Write brand copy by polishing and cutting
foundation_candidates.summary: The source's copy principles: language that resonates with meaning and lets readers layer their own experience, clarity and brevity first, and ruthless cutting.
foundation_candidates.use_when: When writing or editing product descriptions, category copy, emails or ads where length and clarity directly affect comprehension.
steps: Use language that resonates with meaning and expect readers to complete the message with layers of their own experience — this argues for copy that leaves room for the customer rather than over-explaining.
Aim for clarity, brevity and precision on the assumption that a busy reader may have only minutes to spare.
Polish and cut as if you were a jeweler; the source's image is that every sentence should reveal new facets to the customer.
Cut through clutter to produce soundbites that gain identity through repetition — but only repeat lines you are comfortable having associated with the brand long term.

Edit out modifying phrases, adverbs and extraneous conversational text; the source's claim is that what remains is the distillation, the essence, and that eliminating distracting references gives the text impact.
Accept the underlying writing standard the source quotes from Strunk and White: a sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences.
caveats: These are style principles, not measured conversion tactics; the source does not claim brevity itself increases conversion.
Cutting must not remove necessary product information that buyers need for the purchase decision.

foundation_candidates.title: Brand identity as a tangible system that unifies the whole store
foundation_candidates.summary: Brand identity is the visible, tangible system (logo, color, type, imagery, voice) that makes a big idea accessible and recognizable across every customer touchpoint.
foundation_candidates.use_when: When deciding how to express a positioning or 'big idea' across an ecommerce store — homepage, PDP, packaging, emails, ads — and whether your look feels like one coherent brand or several unrelated ones.
steps: Separate the idea from its expression: a brand is the perception customers hold, while brand identity is the tangible system you can see, touch, hold and hear. The identity is what carries the meaning; the meaning itself is intangible.

Treat every element (brandmark, wordmark, color palette, typography, sound, motion) as a component of one system rather than an isolated asset. The source's principle: brand identity takes disparate elements and unifies them into whole systems.
Audit your existing touchpoints against that system. Check whether your logo, product photography, packaging, and email templates look like they come from the same company or from different ones.
Wherever a touchpoint is inconsistent, unify it to the system; the goal is recognition and differentiation, so visual fragmentation directly weakens both.
Remember design is doing the differentiating work — it embodies the intangibles (emotion, context, essence) that customers actually respond to, not just a decorative layer.
caveats: This is a positioning/design principle, not evidence of sales lift; the source asserts design differentiates but offers no measured ecommerce results.
Consistency matters most for recognition, but choosing which elements can flex (see flexibility) is a separate decision.

foundation_note: Inferred principle labels do not establish universal applicability. Retain source conditions; empty means no matched labelled principle, not absence of foundational knowledge.
